item.title: A Homotopic Kuratowski Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2611.28401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that if a map from a graph G to a compact orientable surface, possibly with boundary, cannot be deformed so as to remove all crossings, then neither can its restriction to some subgraph of G with at most 72 vertices of degree other than two. On the sphere, this is Kuratowski's theorem; in contrast, minimal obstructions to embeddability in a surface grow with its genus. Our proof reduces the problem to planarity in a disk with order constraints, and identifies a condition under which this problem has small obstructions. Our main tool is a homotopic version of depth-first search trees, which underlie classical planarity tests and the extraction of Kuratowski subgraphs.
item.dc:creator: Lo\"ic Dubois

item.title: Approximate Map Matching under Realistic Assumptions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and a polygonal curve $P$ of complexity $n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we study the map matching problem of computing a path in $G$ that minimises the Fr\'echet distance to $P$. Chen, Driemel, Guibas, Nguyen and Wenk (ALENEX 2011) gave a near-linear time $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for the case when $G$ is $\lambda$-low-dense and $P$ is $c$-packed. We show that these assumptions can be relaxed, and we give efficient $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms under the weaker conditions. First, if $P$ is $c$-packed and $G$ is an arbitrary graph, we obtain an $\tilde{O}(cn + c^2|E|)$ time algorithm. Second, if both $G$ and $P$ are $\lambda$-low-dense, we obtain an $\tilde{O}(\lambda^2((n|V|)^{1-1/d}+n+|V|))$ expected time algorithm, which becomes $\tilde{O}(\lambda^2(n+|V|))$ in the plane.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Deryckere, Joachim Gudmundsson, Andr\'e van Renssen, Sampson Wong

item.title: Trajectory Visibility at First Sight
item.description: arXiv:2611.29872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, and let two moving entities $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ travel at constant (possibly distinct) speeds $v_q$ and $v_r$ along line-segment trajectories $\tau_q$ and $\tau_r$ inside $P$. We study the first-visibility time $ t^* = \min\bigl\{\,t \ge 0 \mid \overline{q(t)\,r(t)} \subseteq P\,\bigr\}, $ the earliest moment at which the segment joining $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ lies entirely within $P$. Prior work by Eades et al.~\cite{swat2020,eeades-phd} focused on the decision version of this question in a simple polygon. They gave a one-shot decision algorithm running in ${O}(n)$ time. For a stationary entity and a moving one, they gave a data structure with ${O}(n \log n)$ preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that answers decision queries in ${O}(\log n)$ time. For two moving entities, after ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ preprocessing time, they built a data structure of size ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ with ${O}(n^{3/4}\log^3 n)$ query time. Variants for polygonal domains with holes or when entities cross the boundary of $P$ lie beyond our scope. In this work, we go beyond decision to compute $t^*$ exactly under three models for a simple polygon $P$. When both trajectories are fixed in advance, we preprocess $P$ in ${O}(n)$ time and space and answer each query $(v_q, v_r)$ in ${O}(\log n)$ time. If one trajectory $\tau_r$ is fixed while $\tau_q$ is given as a query, we build a structure in ${O}(n \log n)$ time and space that computes $t^*$ in ${O}(\log^2 n)$ time per query. When neither trajectory is known in advance, we develop a data structure with ${O}(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ expected preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that achieves ${O}(n^{1/2}\,\text{polylog}(n))$ expected query time for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Abam, M.A., Ghodsi, M., Kazemi, S.M.H. (2026). Trajectory Visibility at First Sight. In: Di Giacomo, E., Mondal, D. (eds) WALCOM: Algorithms and Computation. WALCOM 2026. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 16444. Springer, Singapore
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Ali Abam, Mohammad Ghodsi, Seyed Mohammad Hussein Kazemi

item.title: Algorithms for Detecting Shape Defects in Concentrated Solar Power Plant Components
item.description: arXiv:2611.30401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Concentrated solar power (CSP) technology offers a dispatchable renewable energy solution, capable of bridging the gap between intermittent generation and grid demand through high-capacity thermal energy storage. However, the overall thermodynamic efficiency and cost-effectiveness of CSP plants depend crucially on the optical quality and precise geometric alignment of thousands of reflective surfaces spread across vast solar fields. Shape defect detection algorithms have become essential tools for automating mirror profilometry, tracking the flow spot and diagnosing alignment issues. This paper presents a novel framework for geometric shape detection techniques tailored to CSP applications. It introduces the notion of \emph{parabolicity}, which motivates a class of optimisation problems in this setting and suggests a possible direction for further work in computational geometry. Both exact and approximate algorithms are proposed, together with an experimental study on synthetic datasets generated via simulation.
item.dc:creator: J. M. D\'iaz-B\'a\~nez, M. Medr\'an-Navarro

item.title: Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.30657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.
item.dc:creator: Paco Navarro, Michael Emmerich

item.title: A 2.05-Approximation for Unit Disk Graph Coloring
item.description: arXiv:2611.31008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The best known approximation ratio for coloring unit disk graphs has been $3$ since the early 1990s. It comes from a left-to-right sweep, in which the earlier neighbors of a vertex are covered by three cliques. We give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, given the points, colors every unit disk graph $G$ with at most $2.05\,\chi(G)$ colors. The algorithm first approximately solves the LP for the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f$. If $\chi_f$ is large, it samples color classes from the LP solution independently in each cell of a coarse grid and colors the remaining vertices with the sweep, reusing a sampled color whenever no neighbor has it. This refines the Round-and-Approx scheme of Bansal, Caprara, and Sviridenko; the new ingredient is locality: a bounded-differences inequality combined with the constructive Lov\'asz Local Lemma controls all residual cliques simultaneously. If $\chi_f$ is small, then so is the clique number, and dynamic programming provides good approximations. Our techniques also improve the best known approximation ratios for intersection graphs of translates of a convex polygon, from $3$ to $2.05$, and for unit square graphs, from $2$ to $1.68$.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme D. da Fonseca, Kunal Dutta

item.title: Online Disk Hitting via Two-Point Traces
item.description: arXiv:2611.31034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the online hitting set problem for disks, a set $P$ of $n$ points in the plane is given in advance, and disks intersecting $P$ arrive one at a time. After each arrival, the algorithm must maintain a hitting set $X\subseteq P$ for all disks seen so far. The algorithm can only add points to $X$, and the objective is to minimize the final size of $X$. Even and Smorodinsky gave an $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for unit disks and asked whether the $O(\log^2 n)$ bound for disks of arbitrary radii could be improved. For arbitrary radii, our randomized algorithm selects $O(k(1+\log(n/k)))$ points in expectation on every fixed request sequence, where $k$ is the size of a minimum hitting set for that sequence. This gives an $O(\log n)$ expected competitive ratio. For every $k$, we prove a matching lower bound on the worst-case expected cost, even on collinear point sets. The algorithm samples priority orders on $P$ in advance. For each arriving disk $D$, it selects the first point of $D\cap P$ in the current order. The same expected cost bound holds for shortest-path balls in graphs excluding a fixed minor, with a matching lower bound on paths.
item.dc:creator: Mingchao Zhou, Chunying Ren, Yingli Ran, Zhao Zhang

item.title: Approximate Minimum Triangle Partitions
item.description: arXiv:2611.31146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $\rho(P)$ be the minimum number of triangles in a partition of a simple polygon $P$ with $n$ vertices where triangle corners may be arbitrary points (Steiner points). It is not known whether $\rho(P)$ can be computed in polynomial time. We do not assume general position: when vertices of $P$ are collinear, a triangle side may pass through several vertices, and good partitions exploit this. Every vertex of $P$ is a corner of some triangle of every partition, so $\rho(P) \ge n/3$, and any triangulation, with $n-2$ triangles, is a 3-approximation that can be computed in $O(n)$ time. This is the best factor known. We improve it in two steps. First, let $\rho_0(P)$ be the minimum number of triangles over partitions whose corners are all vertices of $P$, which can be computed in $O(n^3)$ time (Asano, Asano, and Pinter, 1986). We prove that $\rho_0(P) \le 2\rho(P)-2$ unless $P$ is a triangle, which is tight. Thus Steiner points save at most half of the triangles and $\rho_0(P)$ is a 2-approximation, computed in $O(n^3)$ time. Second, we break the factor-2 barrier of Steiner-free partitions. We observe that $\rho_0(P)$ is close to $2\rho(P)$ only if optimal partitions have few Steiner points, each with many triangles around it. We handle this case by a dynamic program over partitions in which every Steiner point in the interior of $P$ is joined to a vertex of $P$ by a straight run of triangle sides, giving a 5/3-approximation in $O(n^{12})$ time.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme D. da Fonseca

item.title: Improved Lower Bound on the Hadwiger-Debrunner Numbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.29166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The celebrated $(p,q)$-theorem of Alon and Kleitman asserts that for any $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and any $p \geq q \geq d+1$, every family of convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^d$ in which among any $p$ sets, some $q$ intersect, can be pierced by $c(p,q,d)$ points. The minimum numbers $c(p,q,d)$ are called the Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers and denoted $\mathrm{HD}_d(p,q)$ and determining them is a longstanding open problem. We prove that for any $d \geq 2$, $\mathrm{HD}_d(p,d+1) \geq p^{d-o(1)}$, and more generally, $\mathrm{HD}_d(p,q) \geq p^{\frac{q-1}{q-d}-o(1)}$. Our bound is obtained by a family of parallelotopes, and is tight up to polylogarithmic factors among all families that have a bounded VC dimension. The proof uses the hypergraph container method.
item.dc:creator: Chaya Keller

item.title: Area Stability for Largest Small Polygons
item.description: arXiv:2611.29185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a second order calculus for area maximisation among small polygons of diameter at most one, culminating in rigorous computational proofs of stationarity, spectral stability and strict local maximality modulo orientation preserving Euclidean motions for the polygons $Q_n$, whose diameter graphs consist of a cycle on $n-1$ vertices and one pendant edge, for every even $n$ with $6\le n\le 64$. At a stationary configuration, positive multipliers force first order area decrease along feasible directions that shorten at least one active diameter. Along directions that preserve all active diameters to first order, the reduced Hessian governs second order area change modulo Euclidean motions. Positive multipliers, independent active constraint gradients, and a negative reduced spectrum imply strict local maximality. Outward rounded interval arithmetic establishes existence of strictly convex stationary configurations $Q_n$ with all $n-3$ reduced eigenvalues strictly negative. Together, these results yield explicit neighbourhood radii and rigorous quadratic area decrease bounds for all sufficiently nearby feasible polygons. The reduced spectrum also detects second order degeneracy and instability, as illustrated by an optimal quadrilateral and the regular hexagon.
item.dc:creator: Jos\'e Ayala Hoffmann, Joaqu\'in L\'opez Guti\'errez

item.title: Sharp Volume Contraction of a Centrally Cut John Ellipsoid
item.description: arXiv:2611.29323v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ in positive dimension, let $w(K)$ be the volume of its maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid. For a closed halfspace $H$ whose boundary passes through the center of that ellipsoid, we prove \[ w(K\cap H)\le R_nw(K),\qquad R_1=\frac12,\qquad R_n=\frac12\left(\frac n{n-1}\right)^{(n-1)/2}\quad(n\ge2), \] with equality attained in every fixed dimension. This refines the optimal dimension-independent bound from the author's earlier work on [Khachiyan's ellipsoid conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28447). We characterize the full equality family, including nonsimplex extremizers, and establish an exact volume-deficit identity that yields dimension-independent stability of the new ellipsoid and its weighted contact geometry in John coordinates. The proof reduces the problem to finite John contacts and constructs an explicit conic certificate by a transformation of contact directions and a common polar rotation. Its determinant is controlled by a nonnegative contact defect. The sharp contraction theorem, equality classification, stability estimates, and supporting results have been formally verified in Lean 4 using mathlib.
item.dc:creator: Zhou Longfei

item.title: Toward Open Room-Scale Scanning with Consumer LiDAR via Depth-Inertial Odometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.30166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Room scanning with consumer LiDAR today depends on ARKit, whose tracking and map update are a black box: an application receives depth and poses but cannot inspect how they were produced, so an error in a scan cannot be traced to its cause. This paper examines whether an open alternative, one whose every stage can be inspected, is feasible on the device. Mobile-LIO is a depth-inertial odometry pipeline that uses the phone's depth and inertial data and no ARKit poses. On seven ScanNet++ iPhone recordings it completed every scene with 0.2-2.0 m deviation from the ARKit-derived reference, where six open-source LiDAR-inertial estimators run as configured for dedicated scanners had at least 4.46 m in 41 of 42 runs (two of the six also failed a noise-free adapter check, and Mobile-LIO has a speed cap they lack; the comparison is not controlled and does not rone 15 Pro Max, a buildwith corrected phone code kept up with the sensor in 14 of 15 replay runs of three 7-13 s recordings; e estimator before thosecorrections. item.title: Avoiding Distances
item.description: arXiv:2610.24803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given a finite planar point set $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, let $a_1<a_2< \cdots < a_s$ denote the $s \leq {n \choose 2}$ different (Euclidean) distances between points in $X$. The aim is to retain as many of the points as possible such that certain imposed inter-pair distances are avoided. For example, we show that: (A) Given a set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, an independent set of size $0.2293 n$ in the unit distance graph determined by $X$ can be found in $O(n^2)$ time. For any fixed $k \in \mathbf{N}$ there exists a constant $c_k>0$ such that for any set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, and set $D$ of size $k$, there exists a subset $X' \subseteq X$ of size $|X'| \geq c_k |X|$ in which no pair of points is at some distance in $D$ (we say that $X'$ avoids distances in $D$). Such a set can be found efficiently. (B) (i) There is a subset of $X$ of size $n/2$ that avoids the maximum distance; this bound cannot be improved. (ii) There is a subset of $X$ of size $8n/47$ that avoids both the minimum and maximum distance; on the other hand, there exists $X$ such that at most $5n/16$ points can be retained with this property. (iii) There is a subset of $X$ of size $n/7$ whose diameter is at most half the original diameter; on the other hand, there exists $X$ such that at most $n/6$ points can be retained with this property. (C) (i) For any $\varepsilon>0$, a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for \textsc{MIS} in the minimum distance graph of $n$ points in the plane can be found in $2^{O(1/\varepsilon)} n^{O(1)}$ time. (ii) Given a set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, a maximum independent set in the graph of diameters can be computed in $O(n \log{n})$ time. The techniques used to handle the planar case can be extended to $\mathbf{R}^d$ for any fixed dimension $d$.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Dumitrescu, Zsolt L\'angi

item.title: The Containment Polytope of a Triangle and a Convex Polygon
item.description: arXiv:2611.08556v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The containment polytope $\mathcal{C}$ for a triangle $P$ and a convex $n$-gon $Q$ is a four-dimensional polytope representing the similarity transforms (translation, rotation, scaling) that place $P$ inside $Q$. While it is known that the complexity of $\mathcal{C}$ and its silhouette $\Lambda$, which represents all the largest placements of $P$ inside $Q$ for all orientations, can be quadratic in $n$, we show that the silhouette can be partitioned into a linear number of planar convex chains and steps in $O(n \log n)$ time. Based on the linear number of convex chains and steps, we can compute the complexity of silhouette $\Lambda$ in $O(n \log n)$ time and query the largest placement of $P$ inside $Q$ for a given orientation in $O(\log n)$ time. We explain geometrically how the triangle $P$ rotates while continuously scaling and translating to be maximal inside $Q$, leading to a parameterized algorithm for containment problems.
item.dc:creator: Yoonsung Choi, Sunghee Choi

item.title: Two Results on Outer-String Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2605.12253v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An \emph{outer-string representation} of a graph $G$ is an intersection representation of $G$ where vertices are represented by curves (strings) inside the unit disk and each curve has exactly one endpoint on the boundary of the unit disk (the anchor of the curve). Additionally, if each two curves are allowed to cross at most once, we call this an \emph{outer-$1$-string representation} of $G$. If we impose a cyclic ordering on the vertices of $G$ and require the cyclic order of the anchors to respect this cyclic order, such a representation is called a \emph{constrained outer-string representation}. In this paper, we present two results about graphs admitting outer-string representations. Firstly, we show that for a bipartite graph $G$ (and, more generally, for any $\{C_3,C_5\}$-free graph $G$) with a given cyclic order of vertices, we can decide in polynomial time whether $G$ admits a constrained outer-string representation. Our algorithm follows from a characterization by a single forbidden configuration, similar to that of Biedl et al. [GD 2024] for chordal graphs. Secondly, we answer an open question from the same authors and show that determining whether a given graph admits an outer-1-string representation is NP-hard. More generally, we show that it is NP-hard to determine if a given graph $G$ admits an outer-$k$-string representation for any fixed $k\ge1$.
item.dc:creator: Todor Anti\'c, V\'it Jel\'inek, Jan Kratochv\'il, Peter Stumpf
